qs.q:
UNIT 2: HUMANS AND THE ENVIRONMENT — NGỮ PHÁP & TỪ VỰNG (ĐỀ 1): Mark the letter A, B, C, or D on your answer sheet to indicate the correct answer to each of the following questions.
Look at those dark clouds over the schoolyard! It ______ heavily in a few minutes.
qs.ex: Dự đoán có căn cứ rõ ràng ở hiện tại ('Look at those dark clouds!') → dùng 'be going to': is going to rain.

qs.q: More than two thousand reusable cloth bags ______ to shoppers at the local market last Sunday.
qs.ex: Câu bị động thì Quá khứ đơn ('last Sunday'): were given.

qs.q: Turning off electrical appliances when they are not in use helps reduce our carbon ______.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 2: carbon footprint = dấu chân carbon / lượng khí thải carbon.

qs.q: Wait a minute! That recycling box looks too heavy for you—I ______ you carry it to the gate.
qs.ex: Quyết định tức thời tại thời điểm nói ('Wait a minute!') → dùng 'will + V0': will help.

qs.q: Choosing ______ vegetables grown without chemical pesticides is good for both your health and the soil.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 2: organic vegetables = rau hữu cơ.

qs.q: Every Friday afternoon, our school playground ______ by the Go Green Club members.
qs.ex: Câu bị động thì Hiện tại đơn ('Every Friday afternoon... by the Go Green Club members'): is cleaned.

qs.q: We have already bought fifty young trees. We ______ them around the school fence this Saturday morning.
qs.ex: Kế hoạch đã có sự chuẩn bị trước ('have already bought fifty young trees') → dùng 'be going to': are going to plant.

qs.q: Single-use plastic bottles take hundreds of years to ______ down in landfills.
qs.ex: Phrasal verb Unit 2: break down = phân hủy.

qs.q: Household waste should ______ into organic waste, recyclables and general rubbish before collection.
qs.ex: Bị động với modal verb: should be sorted (được phân loại).

qs.q: Using public transport instead of private cars cuts ______ on harmful greenhouse gas emissions.
qs.ex: Phrasal verb Unit 2: cut down on = cắt giảm.

qs.q: A new solar-panel system ______ on the roof of our school library next month.
qs.ex: Bị động tương lai đơn ('next month'): will be installed.

qs.q: Bringing your own refillable water bottle to school is a simple way to live a ______ lifestyle.
qs.ex: Cụm từ Unit 2: live a green lifestyle = sống xanh.

qs.q: Don't throw those glass jars away! They can ______ to store dried beans and spices.
qs.ex: Câu bị động: can be reused (có thể được tái sử dụng).

qs.q: I think more people ______ electric bicycles in our town in the next ten years.
qs.ex: Dự đoán tương lai có 'I think... in the next ten years' → dùng 'will + V0': will use.

qs.q: Collecting old paper and aluminium cans for recycling helps conserve natural ______.
qs.ex: Cụm từ Unit 2: natural resources = tài nguyên thiên nhiên.

qs.q:
Mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best arrangement of utterances or sentences to make a cohesive and coherent exchange or text in each of the following questions from 7 to 11.
**Dear Alex,**
a. At school, our teachers also organise practical projects to help us cut down on single-use plastic waste and save energy.
b. Thank you for your email; it was great to hear about your recent school activities.
c. At weekends, my friends and I join community groups to adopt an eco-friendly lifestyle in our community.
d. I’m writing to tell you about how we are learning about adopting a green lifestyle and reducing our carbon footprint in Unit 2: Humans and the Environment.
e. Write back soon and tell me what your school is doing on this topic!
**Best wishes,**
qs.ex: Trình tự bức thư: Cảm ơn thư trước (b) → Nêu lý do viết thư chia sẻ chủ đề Unit (d) → Kể hoạt động ở trường (a) → Kể hoạt động cuối tuần (c) → Lời kết thư (e): b - d - a - c - e.

qs.q:
a. Nam: Yes, definitely! Let’s sign up together after class today.
b. Mai: Nam, our school club is holding a workshop on adopting a green lifestyle and reducing our carbon footprint this Saturday. Would you like to join?
c. Mai: Great! I’ll get two registration forms from the club leader.
qs.ex: Trình tự hội thoại 3 lượt: Mai rủ Nam tham gia workshop chủ đề Unit (b) → Nam đồng ý đăng ký (a) → Mai nói sẽ đi lấy phiếu đăng ký (c): b - a - c.

qs.q:
a. To address this, schools and communities are now launching new green habits in our community.
b. In the past, many people did not pay enough attention to adopting a green lifestyle and reducing our carbon footprint.
c. Today, however, both citizens and students realise how important it is to adopt an eco-friendly lifestyle.
d. As a result, everyone benefits when we work together to reduce our household carbon footprint and protect local ecosystems.
e. These practical programmes help participants cut down on single-use plastic waste and save energy in their daily lives.
qs.ex: Trình tự đoạn văn 5 câu: Thực trạng trước đây (b) → Nhận thức thay đổi ngày nay (c) → Giải pháp triển khai chương trình mới (a) → Tác dụng của các chương trình đó ('These practical programmes') (e) → Kết quả chung (d): b - c - a - e - d.

qs.q:
a. Linh: I’m preparing a poster about adopting a green lifestyle and reducing our carbon footprint for our English lesson tomorrow.
b. Minh: That sounds interesting! What main benefit are you highlighting on the poster?
c. Minh: Well done, Linh. I’m sure our classmates will learn a lot from your presentation!
d. Linh: I’m focusing on how green habits can cut down on single-use plastic waste and save energy and reduce our household carbon footprint and protect local ecosystems.
e. Minh: What are you working on, Linh? You look really focused.
qs.ex: Trình tự hội thoại 5 lượt: Minh hỏi Linh đang làm gì (e) → Linh nói đang làm poster cho bài học tiếng Anh (a) → Minh hỏi lợi ích chính trên poster là gì (b) → Linh giải thích nội dung (d) → Minh khen ngợi (c): e - a - b - d - c.

qs.q:
a. Next, participants work in small groups to discuss practical ways to adopt an eco-friendly lifestyle.
b. After the opening talk, the organisers show a short video on how green habits work in our community.
c. Every month, our youth club organises a special morning session dedicated to adopting a green lifestyle and reducing our carbon footprint.

**PERSPECTIVES ON HUMANS AND THE ENVIRONMENT**
In recent years, adopting a green lifestyle and reducing our carbon footprint has attracted growing attention from educators and researchers alike. A recent national survey reports that while over eighty per cent of citizens and students recognise the importance of green habits, only about thirty-five per cent have <u>**reduced**</u> these practices into their daily routines in our community. Even when resources are available, many people still struggle to balance their busy schedules with the need to adopt an eco-friendly lifestyle.
The challenge lies not only in awareness but also in daily habits. Researchers note that active participants regularly engage in structured tasks that cut down on single-use plastic waste and save energy, whereas passive observers only join occasional events once or twice a year. Consistent practice requires patience and planning, but it delivers lasting rewards. Many individuals simply repeat outdated habits they observed in the past, which prevents them from experiencing how green habits can reduce our household carbon footprint and protect local ecosystems.
Fortunately, attitudes are shifting rapidly. **[I]** Most respondents in the survey agreed that everyone should adopt an eco-friendly lifestyle, even though many admitted spending less than two hours a week on it themselves. **[II]** Progress was strongest in communities where schools and families worked together as partners. **[III]** Groups can begin by setting clear weekly goals and giving every member a practical role in our community. **[IV]** Small, steady steps like these can turn a difficult challenge into a shared habit of cooperation.
Promoting adopting a green lifestyle and reducing our carbon footprint matters for the long-term future. Young people who see citizens and students model positive behaviours are likely to view these practices as normal, and <u>**they**</u> will carry those values into adulthood. In this way, green habits not only cut down on single-use plastic waste and save energy today but also reduce our household carbon footprint and protect local ecosystems for generations to come.
(Adapted from Educational & Social Research Reports – Unit 2: Humans and the Environment)

Citizens and students can start with simple steps in our community, share responsibilities and use practical checklists to stay on track. Those who understand the purpose behind adopting a green lifestyle and reducing our carbon footprint become much more resilient and motivated.
Of course, no single workshop or rule will solve every challenge overnight, and some groups need time to adapt. That is no reason to give up. Even one or two focused sessions a week can spark meaningful change, and the positive <u>**lifestyle**</u> will grow stronger over time. **PARTNERSHIPS BETWEEN SCHOOLS AND FAMILIES IN UNIT 2: HUMANS AND THE ENVIRONMENT**
Over the past two years, a research team from the National Institute of Education has tracked 1,500 high school students to evaluate how adopting a green lifestyle and reducing our carbon footprint affects teenager development. The study found that while nearly ninety per cent of citizens and students valued green habits, only forty-two per cent <u>**sustained**</u> these routines throughout the entire school year. Students who tried to practise alone often gave up after a few weeks when exam pressure increased.
By contrast, learners whose families and teachers coordinated their guidance achieved far more durable results. In households where parents actively joined weekend activities to adopt an eco-friendly lifestyle in our community, teenagers were twice as likely to cut down on single-use plastic waste and save energy. Researchers explained that shared routines reduce the feeling of isolation and turn abstract classroom advice into enjoyable daily habits. Moreover, consistent family involvement helps reduce our household carbon footprint and protect local ecosystems without adding extra stress to students’ timetables.
Schools across the country are now redesigning their programmes based on these findings. **[I]** Instead of assigning theoretical worksheets, teachers invite parents and students to co-sign a simple weekly action plan. **[II]** This joint commitment ensures that classroom lessons are reinforced at home every evening. **[III]** At monthly review sessions, classes celebrate collective progress and exchange practical solutions to common obstacles. **[IV]**
The long-term implications of this partnership model are encouraging. When citizens and students work side by side, <u>**they**</u> build mutual respect and lasting life skills. Ultimately, integrating adopting a green lifestyle and reducing our carbon footprint into both school curricula and family life prepares young citizens to thrive in an increasingly complex world.
(Adapted from National Educational Research Reports – Unit 2: Humans and the Environment)

**WHY CONSISTENCY MATTERS MORE THAN PERFECTION IN UNIT 2: HUMANS AND THE ENVIRONMENT**
When people first decide to focus on adopting a green lifestyle and reducing our carbon footprint, they often set overly ambitious targets. Enthusiastic beginners might promise to transform their entire lifestyle in a single weekend, only to feel exhausted a few days later. Studies on habit formation show that well-paced green habits are far more effective when built step by step, helping citizens and students cut down on single-use plastic waste and save energy without burnout.
The main reason crash campaigns fail is that <u>**they**</u> demand too much willpower at once. <u>**Small, consistent efforts practised every day produce far more lasting results than occasional bursts of intense activity.**</u> When a routine fits naturally into a family’s or student’s daily schedule, it requires less mental strain to maintain.
Experts therefore recommend a <u>**gradual**</u> approach to adopt an eco-friendly lifestyle in our community. By starting with one simple task each day and celebrating weekly milestones, learners steadily build momentum. Such steady practice not only strengthens personal discipline but also helps communities reduce our household carbon footprint and protect local ecosystems.
Of course, occasional setbacks are normal during busy exam weeks or family events. Rather than abandoning the goal altogether, resilient learners simply resume their routine the next morning, knowing that patience will <u>**foster**</u> long-term success.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 2: Humans and the Environment)

**COMMUNITY ACTION AND PEER MENTORING IN UNIT 2: HUMANS AND THE ENVIRONMENT**
Last year, youth unions in three provinces launched a six-month pilot programme to promote adopting a green lifestyle and reducing our carbon footprint at the grassroots level. Instead of relying on formal lectures, organisers trained two hundred high school volunteers to lead weekend activities where neighbours could adopt an eco-friendly lifestyle in our community. Within the first two months, local communities reported <u>**tangible**</u> improvements in daily habits and neighbourhood solidarity.
A key factor behind this success was peer-to-peer mentoring. Teenagers often feel intimidated when adults lecture them, but they respond enthusiastically when classmates demonstrate how green habits can cut down on single-use plastic waste and save energy. By working in small teams of five or six, participants shared practical tips, solved everyday problems together and helped one another reduce our household carbon footprint and protect local ecosystems.
Organisers also introduced simple tools to keep momentum high. **[I]** Every participating household received a visual progress board to track weekly milestones. **[II]** Local cultural centres hosted monthly gatherings where teams showcased their most creative ideas. **[III]** These celebrations turned routine tasks into a source of shared pride across the entire district. **[IV]**
Follow-up surveys conducted six months later confirmed that over seventy-five per cent of participants continued practising green habits independently. When student volunteers take ownership of community initiatives, <u>**their**</u> enthusiasm inspires both younger children and older residents. The pilot programme demonstrates that youth-led action is one of the most powerful ways to bring the values of Unit 2: Humans and the Environment to life.
(Adapted from Community Development & Youth Studies – Unit 2: Humans and the Environment)

**THE RIPPLE EFFECT OF PEER LEADERSHIP IN UNIT 2: HUMANS AND THE ENVIRONMENT**
How do positive habits spread across a school or neighbourhood? Sociologists studying adopting a green lifestyle and reducing our carbon footprint have discovered that peer influence is often stronger than formal rules. When citizens and students see their close friends willingly engage in green habits, they are far more likely to join in and cut down on single-use plastic waste and save energy.
Nevertheless, launching a new initiative is never without challenges. Organisers note that initial doubts and busy routines are common, and <u>**they**</u> can slow down participation during the first week. <u>**Young people learn most effectively when they observe respected peers applying positive habits in real-life situations.**</u>
For this reason, many schools encourage <u>**voluntary**</u> student ambassadors to lead by example. Whether demonstrating how to adopt an eco-friendly lifestyle in our community or sharing practical tips during break time, these role models create a welcoming ripple effect that helps the whole school reduce our household carbon footprint and protect local ecosystems.
Even when a minor <u>**obstacle**</u> arises, a supportive peer group keeps members motivated. What begins as the effort of a few enthusiastic students soon grows into a proud tradition shared by the entire community.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 2: Humans and the Environment)

**OVERCOMING BARRIERS TO DAILY PRACTICE IN UNIT 2: HUMANS AND THE ENVIRONMENT**
Why do many high school students agree that adopting a green lifestyle and reducing our carbon footprint is important, yet still find it difficult to adopt an eco-friendly lifestyle in our community every day? Educational psychologists point out that modern teenagers face three main barriers: digital distractions, academic pressure and a lack of structured routines. When students feel overwhelmed, they often become <u>**reluctant**</u> to take on new responsibilities at home or in the community.
Fortunately, behavioural research shows that breaking large goals into micro-habits can overcome this hesitation. Instead of trying to change everything overnight, citizens and students can start with a fifteen-minute daily routine focused on green habits. These manageable actions quickly build confidence and help learners cut down on single-use plastic waste and save energy without interfering with their homework.
Another effective strategy is using a structured weekly checklist. **[I]** When teenagers write down specific times and places for their tasks, they are three times more likely to follow through. **[II]** Sharing <u>**it**</u> with a supportive classmate or family member adds friendly accountability. **[III]** Rather than feeling pressured, students enjoy tracking their streak of completed tasks and seeing how their efforts reduce our household carbon footprint and protect local ecosystems. **[IV]**
Teachers who have introduced micro-habits and checklists into their lessons on Unit 2: Humans and the Environment report remarkable improvements in student engagement. Once young people realise that small daily choices lead to meaningful results, green habits stops feeling like a burden and becomes a natural part of who they are.
(Adapted from Adolescent Psychology & Education Review – Unit 2: Humans and the Environment)

**EXPERIENTIAL LEARNING AND THE FUTURE OF UNIT 2: HUMANS AND THE ENVIRONMENT**
Across Viet Nam, forward-thinking high schools are transforming how students learn about adopting a green lifestyle and reducing our carbon footprint. Rather than treating Unit 2: Humans and the Environment as a set of vocabulary items to memorise for a test, teachers are integrating experiential learning into every week of the semester. Educators agree that hands-on practice is <u>**indispensable**</u> if young people are to cut down on single-use plastic waste and save energy.
In these classrooms, students work in project teams to investigate real issues and propose ways to adopt an eco-friendly lifestyle in our community. For instance, learners might interview local residents, design bilingual awareness posters or organise a school-wide campaign on green habits. Through these authentic tasks, citizens and students discover how their classroom English connects directly to everyday life.
Assessment methods are evolving alongside teaching styles. **[I]** Instead of relying solely on written quizzes, schools evaluate how effectively students collaborate and apply their plans. **[II]** Each team keeps a reflective portfolio documenting the challenges they faced and how their actions helped reduce our household carbon footprint and protect local ecosystems. **[III]** This approach rewards creativity, persistence and genuine teamwork rather than rote memorisation. **[IV]**
Graduates of experiential programmes consistently report higher confidence when entering university and the workplace. Students <u>**who**</u> have practised solving real-world problems in high school adapt much faster to new environments. By making adopting a green lifestyle and reducing our carbon footprint an active, lived experience, education equips the next generation with both language proficiency and civic responsibility.
(Adapted from Modern Curriculum & Pedagogy Journal – Unit 2: Humans and the Environment)

**EXPERIENTIAL LEARNING AND THE FUTURE OF UNIT 2: HUMANS AND THE ENVIRONMENT**
Across Viet Nam, forward-thinking high schools are transforming how students learn about adopting a green lifestyle and reducing our carbon footprint. Rather than treating Unit 2: Humans and the Environment as a set of vocabulary items to memorise for a test, teachers are integrating experiential learning into every week of the semester. Educators agree that hands-on practice is <u>**indispensable**</u> if young people are to cut down on single-use plastic waste and save energy.
In these classrooms, students work in project teams to investigate real issues and propose ways to adopt an eco-friendly lifestyle in our community. For instance, learners might interview local residents, design bilingual awareness posters or organise a school-wide campaign on green habits. Through these authentic tasks, citizens and students discover how their classroom English connects directly to everyday life.
Assessment methods are evolving alongside teaching styles. **[I]** Instead of relying solely on written quizzes, schools evaluate how effectively students collaborate and apply their plans. **[II]** Each team keeps a reflective portfolio documenting the challenges they faced and how their actions helped reduce our household carbon footprint and protect local ecosystems. **[III]** This approach rewards creativity, persistence and genuine teamwork rather than rote memorisation. **[IV]**
Graduates of experiential programmes consistently report higher confidence when entering university and the workplace. Students <u>**who**</u> have practised solving real-world problems in high school adapt much faster to new environments. By making adopting a green lifestyle and reducing our carbon footprint an active, lived experience, education equips the next generation with both language proficiency and civic responsibility.
(Adapted from Modern Curriculum & Pedagogy Journal – Unit 2: Humans and the Environment)

**SELF-REFLECTION AND LONG-TERM GROWTH IN UNIT 2: HUMANS AND THE ENVIRONMENT**
Practising green habits is even more rewarding when learners take a few minutes each week to reflect on their progress. Educators studying adopting a green lifestyle and reducing our carbon footprint have found that students who keep a brief weekly journal understand their own habits much better and find it easier to cut down on single-use plastic waste and save energy.
During busy weeks, people sometimes miss a planned task or make mistakes. Without reflection, <u>**they**</u> may feel discouraged and assume that their efforts have failed. <u>**Honest self-reflection allows learners to turn early mistakes into valuable lessons rather than reasons to give up.**</u>
To make reflection effective, teachers recommend asking <u>**constructive**</u> questions every Sunday evening: What went well when we tried to adopt an eco-friendly lifestyle in our community this week, and what small adjustment will help us improve next week?
Over time, this simple habit deepens personal <u>**commitment**</u> and helps citizens and students reduce our household carbon footprint and protect local ecosystems with confidence and pride.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 2: Humans and the Environment)
